Black is a piece down, but the c4 pawn is ready to promote. White's king sits on g1 with the queen on d2, but the queen itself is not yet ready for the queen. White's knight on g6 is already attacking the black king on g8, and the rook on f7 controls the entire seventh rank. Black's knight on d6 and rook on f7 are well-placed to attack the white king on e5, but the king can simply step away to e6. Black's king is hemmed in on g2 while White's king is exposed on f2, and the pawn on g4 is undefended. Capturing with Qxg4 wins material but gives White time to consolidate. White is in check from the rook on a8 but must act before the queen on b5 can reach checkmate. R1d7+ gives check but after Black's king captures the rook the king finds a square to escape. White has two rooks and a bishop against Black's rook on c8, rook on d8, and bishop on g6, but the black king on f6 is dangerously exposed. White has a rook on e1 bearing down on d1. One option is Nh4, a quiet rook sacrifice that allows Rxe5, but then d1 would fall under check from the c3-rook and the winning material balance collapses entirely. Nh4+ is also a forcing rook, yet instead Kf8# delivers an immediate checkmate, with the bishop on c3 covering g7. So the move is Nh4+.

White has a rook on d4 and a queen on b3, with the black king on g8 hemmed in by its own pieces. Rxd8 wins the rook but Black immediately recaptures with the queen, trading the rook and losing a key piece. Qxg6+ captures the pawn but the king escapes to f7 and the attack stalls. The queen sacrifice Qxb3+ forces the king to f7, and the rook on d4 then delivers checkmate: the queen covers f8, the rook controls the entire fourth rank, and the knight on h4 is pinned to the king. So the move is Qxb3+.

Black has a rook on h4 bearing down on d1, which is currently protected only by the a6 rook—White can capture it in a decisive game. Candidate Rxa4 captures the c-pawn but gives White the first decisive shot: a pawn moves, and the queen on b3 fires to h2, threatening to capture on c1. The rook undercuts d2 so White does not see any safe square. Another try, e4, lets White press the position further but also allows c7 and thus maintains the pawn advance. Only Rxa4 removes the rook blocking c1, leaving White with d1 vacated but nothing more to pull. Black wins decisive material on a small but clean initiative.

Widaqs the knight to c4, delivering checkmate on the spot. White's king remains on d2 while the queen on a4 covers the back rank, the knight on c4 attacks b7, and the rook on c2 controls b7 as well. Black's queen and bishops dominate the open position, but the bishop on f2 is the only one accused of guarding the back rank. Black's rook offers no shelter along the long diagonal from c2 to b2. White's queen on a4 and rook on c2 seal off every escape, ending the game immediately. Qxa6+ would be fine check, but it lets Black escape by recapturing on a6, prolonging the game. Material is roughly even, but White's queen on e7 holds the initiative, and Black must act immediately. Qa4+ seems tempting—White can simply recapture or the king sidesteps—and Black only gets a passive check without immediate mate. Bc8+ is another try, but White can capture the bishop or recapture on f8 and the king has the space to stay safe. The queen on a2 can reach f2 in one step, and that square is covered by the bishop on g7: every square adjacent to f2 is defended by the queen or the knight on f2, with the king on g1 completely sealed in by its own pawns. So the move is Qf2#.

Black needs to act decisively to turn the tide. Grabbing the b-pawn with check fails immediately, giving White time to reorganize and keep the initiative. After Black moves the f-pawn to f3, the g2 pawn captures it, eliminating the obstruction while simultaneously proclaiming that the check from e6 is forced, as the rook on e6 is available and the honeycomb mates instantly. With Rxe1 the recapture wins a dangerous rook while Black's passed c5 and e5 pieces are supported by the bishop on b7 — all development and activity together. Black is in check from the white rook on c3 and must find an immediate escape. A simple retreat to Re1 gives up the rook for a knight, leaving White material advantage. The key observation is that the rook lands on c1, delivering check from square with the knight on d4 unable to intervene, because the knight covers c1's only flight square and no White piece can reach there. Black has a queen on h5 and a rook on f8 bearing down on White's king on f4, but the king is already in check from the queen on d1. Qb1# exploits every available flight square, leaving no legal move. Qa2+ only drives the king to e1, but after that the king has escape routes and no mate follows. Black's king is completely trapped with no flight squares. This is the fastest and most decisive continuation of the rook sacrifice.

White has a rook on e1 bearing down on the Black king on c8, backed by the queen on e4 and bishop on f4. Bxe7 wins the bishop but hands Black time to recapture with the king or queen, allowing the game to drag on without forcing mate. Bg5 also gives check but the king can step to d8, d7, or f7 and escape. White is in check from the rook on a1, and the king is on c8. Black is in check from the white king on h5, and the king is on the verge of a checkmate. Black is up material but needs a decisive blow. The white king on c1 is hemmed in by its own pawns on b2 and c2, and the knight on b6 is pinned to the king by the rook on b7. No White piece can intervene, so the king is left stranded with no further legal move. So the move is Qxf7+.

With the black king on c8 confined to the corner, the bishop on f4 is pinned to the c7 square by the queen on c6, which attacks it directly. Moving the bishop to a6 gives check but Black can simply capture the bishop with the rook, defusing the attack. Nd5 would give check too, but after the king takes the knight the position remains messy and Black has many defensive resources. White has a knight on b1 and a bishop on b4 bearing down on the kingside, while Black's queen on d8 is the only active piece. Nd6+ gives check, but Black can recapture the knight and the attack dissipates. Qxd5 wins a pawn but Black recaptures and the queen is gone. So the move is Be7#.

White is in check from the queen on d6, but the black king is on c8. Black's queen on e1 and the g6 and h7 pawns are too far to help the king escape. Capturing on g6 with check is tempting, but after the king moves to b7 or g7 the attack runs out of steam, and Black's queen on e1 will keep pressure. Black has a queen on f5 and a pawn on g6 bearing down on White's king on h1, but the queen on f3 is pinned to the king by the pawn on h3. Black is a piece down, but the passed g5 pawn is one step from promotion. White is in check from the rook on a8, and the king is on e8. Black's queen on d8 and the bishop on f8 are both aimed at the king. Qxf6+ looks tempting as it gives check, but after the king captures on f6 the knight on e7 and rook on a8 slip free, and Black's king is simply one step from escape. White's king on b5 and the h6 pawn are both advanced, but the black king on e5 is completely boxed in by its own pieces. White is ahead in material and the rook on g7 bears on the queen on c2, which Black's king is stranded on h4. The position is a pawn endgame where White's king sits on h2, guarded only by the knight on d8. Black has the queen on b1 and the bishop on c1. The white queen on h5 and rook on h7 converge on Black's bishop on c8, and with the king on g8 staring the rooks in, an immediate reply by check with a rook strike fails—Black captures the rook or king and White is attacked. White is in check from the rook on f5 but must keep things straight, while the g-pawn on d4 can help. So the move is Rb7.

White's queen on g5 dominates and is perfectly placed for a finishing blow. Qxg6+ gives check, but Black's king simply escapes to e8 and the attack stalls. White has a rook on f1 bearing down on d1 while the Black king on c8 is hemmed in by its own pawns on b6, d7, and e6. Rxc1+ gives check but the king simply steps away and there is no forced mate. So the move is gxh7#.

Black's g5-pawn has advanced to b6 while White's king sits on c4 with only f3 and f5 blocked by its own pawns, so the decision is between advancing or promoting. Then the g-pawn captures the f3-pawn immediately, delivering checkmate: after the king retreats to d4 the f3-pawn steps to d4 to complete the invasion, and no White piece can block. White has a rook on e8 bearing down on e1. The Closed anfions are Kc4, gxf6, and a dangerous recomposition driven by Bc4, so no piece is to do this straightforward material risk. White has two rooks bearing down on the black king on h6, with the g8 rook already aimed at g5. Material is roughly even, but White's position is decisive: Black's king is completely boxed in on h8 with the bishop on g7 controlling g8, the rook on g8 defending the g-file, and Black's own king cannot reach safety. Black has a queen, bishop, and knight with followed pawns on a7 and c7 and a rook on a1, all stranded, but the white king on h1 is in no defense. White has a knight on g5 and a bishop on c4 bearing down on the Black king on h8, but the king is completely trapped in the corner with no escape. Black is in check from the white king on e1 but must act before the queen on g2 can reach f3. Black has a rook on d2 and a pawn on g6, but the white king on f1 is completely undefended. Black's knight on h3 is poised to leap to f2, but the white queen on c2 is already active and the king on h1 is dangerously exposed.
